docs.title: Words to know
docs.text:
Word Means Wheelbase The motor the steering wheel attaches to. It makes the force feedback Direct drive Wheel bolted straight to the motor. Smooth, quiet, detailed. The standard now Nm Wheelbase strength. 5 is light, 12 is plenty Load cell A brake pedal that reads how hard you press, not how far Rig The frame that holds seat, wheel and pedals
  • The rest: Glossary

docs.title: F1 Arcade vs home
docs.text: F1 Arcade Home Motion D-BOX actuators under a Vesaro rig None until Tier 5 Wheel and pedals Mid-range Same class or better from Tier 3 Game Custom rFactor 2, heavy driving assists Any sim, fewer assists. Harder at first. Normal Racing Friends, short sprints Any car, any track, ranked races against real people Cost ~$20 to $45 a visit, before food and drink Hardware once, then games

docs.title: Three decisions, in order
docs.text:
• Platform: PC, PlayStation or Xbox. It limits which wheels work before budget does
  • Space: desk only, fold away, or permanent
  • Budget: pick the tier

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Spend order: direct drive wheelbase first, then a load cell brake, then everything else
  • 5 to 8 Nm is plenty to start. 12 Nm is the sweet spot. 10 to 15 Nm covers nearly everyone
  • Direct drive now starts at ~$260. Skip gear-driven wheels unless used
  • Used Logitech G29 at ~$120 resells for ~$120: a free trial
  • PlayStation is the expensive platform at every tier
  • Motion and big torque add immersion, not lap time

docs.title: The six tiers
docs.text: Tier Cost Mount Wheel Brake Screen 0: Desk Starter $200 to $400 Desk clamp 2 to 5.5 Nm Spring Yours 1: Foldable / Apartment $500 to $700 Folding seat or stand 4 to 5.5 Nm direct drive Spring Yours 2: First Dedicated Rig $1,200 to $1,600 Steel cockpit or budget profile 8 to 9 Nm Entry load cell Yours 3: Sweet Spot Enthusiast $1,800 to $2,200 Aluminum profile 12 Nm Good load cell Yours 4: Triples / VR Enthusiast $3,500 to $5,500 Aluminum profile 12 to 21 Nm Good load cell Triples or VR 5: Motion / Pro $10,000 to $18,000 Profile on motion actuators 25 Nm Active Triples or VR

docs.title: Basic constraints
docs.text:
• Platform
    • PC: everything works, every game
    • Xbox: Moza R3, Fanatec with an Xbox wheel, Logitech, Thrustmaster
    • PlayStation: only Logitech, Thrustmaster, Fanatec GT DD Pro and ClubSport DD+. Costs more at every tier
    • Console: one screen, no triples, no iRacing. VR only on PlayStation (PS VR2, Gran Turismo 7)
  • Space
    • Desk only: Tier 0
    • Must fold away: Tier 1. Folded ~104×93×30 cm
    • Permanent: ~2.0×1.0 m for a rig and single screen
    • Triples: ~1.8 to 2.1 m wide
  • Neighbors and housemates
    • Gear wheels rattle. Direct drive is quiet
    • Bass shakers and motion travel through floors
  • PC power
    • Single 1440p screen: ~$1,150 PC
    • Ultrawide, entry triples, Quest VR: ~$1,850 to $2,200 PC
    • Triple 1440p, most VR: ~$3,200 PC. Pimax Dream Air class: more
  • Time
    • Tier 0 and 1 need setup every session. Friction kills the habit
    • A permanent rig gets used more

docs.title: What each jump buys
docs.text:
• 0 to 1: pedals and seat stop moving
  • 1 to 2: nothing flexes, brake by pressure. Consistency
  • 2 to 3: a rig and pedals you never replace
  • 3 to 4: you can see beside you. Immersion
  • 4 to 5: the seat moves. Feel, not speed

docs.title: Cheapest path through the tiers
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Moza R5 bundle<br>on your desk<br>$380] --> B[Load cell pedals<br>$369]
    B --> C[Aluminum rig<br>+ seat + mount<br>~$740]
    C --> D[12 Nm base<br>+ wheel<br>$658]
    D --> E[Triples or VR<br>$600 to $900]
  • Total ~$2,750 to $3,050
  • Order: direct drive first, load cell brake second, then everything else
  • Load cell before the rig: brake set light, chair blocked, pedals against a wall
  • The 12 Nm base is optional. 5 to 8 Nm lasts years
  • Lost on outgrown parts: ~$150 to $250 (est)
  • vs G29, then foldable, then steel cockpit: ~$500 to $900 lost (est)
  • Skip Tier 1 unless it truly must fold away
  • Skip the Tier 2 steel cockpit if the floor space exists
  • PlayStation: no cheap direct drive first step. Used G29, or straight to a Logitech RS50 or Fanatec GT DD Pro

docs.title: $200–$400
docs.text: Assumes: existing PC/console, display, desk

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• Curious after F1 Arcade, want to try a wheel at home for minimum money
  • Shared room, no dedicated space
  • Not sure it will stick
  • Skip if: desk is wobbly or glass
  • Skip if: already sure you want a rig (go to Tier 2)

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• PC: Moza R5 bundle ~$380. 5.5 Nm direct drive, wheel, 2 pedals, desk clamp
  • PC, newer: Moza R5 Pro bundle $399. 6 Nm, newer base and pedals. Take it if the gap is small
  • PC, cheaper: Moza R3 bundle ~$260 to $280. 3.9 Nm direct drive
  • Xbox: Moza R3 Xbox bundle ~$320 to $340
  • PlayStation or Xbox, cheapest: Logitech G29 (PlayStation) / G920 (Xbox) ~$180 to $200 street. Gear drive, 3 pedals. $300 list, never pay list
  • PlayStation, smoother: Thrustmaster T248R $300 (belt / gear hybrid, 3 pedals)
  • No PlayStation direct drive at this price
  • Not in the box: shifter (Logitech $60). Not needed to start

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• Your desk. Wheel clamps to the front edge
  • Pedals on the floor, against a wall or a box
  • Packs away into one box
  • 10 to 15 min to set up the first time. A few minutes each session after (est)

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• vs F1 Arcade: no motion, no fixed seat, fewer assists. Harder at first
  • Logitech G29: notchy, loud gear rattle
  • Moza R3/R5: smooth, quiet, light
  • Slower than a controller for the first week or two
  • Unlimited seat time

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: cheapest way in, nothing to build
  • +: resells easily
  • +: Moza parts bolt onto any rig later
  • −: office chair rolls back under braking
  • −: pedals slide on hard floor
  • −: brake is a spring, not a load cell
  • −: clamp on, clamp off every session. Friction kills the habit

docs.title: Free fixes
docs.text:
• Chair: caster cups, or rear wheels in old shoes
  • Pedals: against the wall, or screwed to a board the chair sits on
  • Desk shake: push desk to wall, lower force feedback

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Load cell brake first: Moza SRP2 pedals $149. Stopgap: Moza brake kit $39
  • On a desk: brake set light, chair blocked, pedals against the wall
  • Then stop things moving: wheel stand or foldable (Tier 1), or a rig (Tier 2)
  • Carries over: Moza base, wheel, pedals
  • Does not carry over: Logitech and T248 sets are closed systems, sold whole. Their next step is a direct drive bundle

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• G29/G920 ~$100 to $150 local
  • Resells for what you paid: a free trial
  • Check: centers on power-up, no grinding, all pedals reach full range, power brick included
  • Avoid: G27 and older (no PS5/Xbox), anything without force feedback

docs.title: $500–$700
docs.text:
Assumes: existing PC/console, display, foldable space

  • PlayStation with direct drive: $900 to $1,100

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• Hooked after Tier 0, or sure you'll stick with it
  • Apartment / shared room, rig must disappear
  • Console on a couch TV
  • Skip if: a 60×140 cm floor spot can be permanent. A fixed cockpit costs $100 to $200 more than a foldable and does not flex (Tier 2)
  • Skip if: you want a stiff load cell brake (foldables flex)

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• PC: Moza R5 bundle ~$380 + NLR GTLite Pro $299 = ~$680
  • PC, newer: R5 Pro bundle $399 in place of the R5. 6 Nm
  • PC, budget: R5 bundle + NLR GTLite $199 = ~$580
  • PC, own chair: R5 bundle + NLR Wheel Stand Lite 2.0 $179 = ~$560
  • Xbox: Moza R3 Xbox bundle ~$340 + Playseat Challenge X $300 = ~$640
  • PlayStation, direct drive: Thrustmaster T598 $600 (5 Nm, wheel, pedals) + GTLite Pro $299 = ~$900
  • PlayStation, r/simracing pick: Logitech RS50 + RS pedals ~$700 to $800 + GTLite Pro $299 = ~$1,000 to $1,100
  • PlayStation, in budget: Thrustmaster T248R $300 + GTLite $199 = ~$500. Not direct drive
  • Newest and cheapest foldable: NLR GTLite Air $179 (Sept 2026)

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• GTLite Pro in use: 176×93×95 cm, 14.4 kg
  • Folded: 104×93×30 cm. Closet, not under the bed
  • Challenge X: 11.6 kg
  • First assembly 30 to 60 min (est)
  • Fold or unfold with gear attached: 1 to 2 min (est)

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• vs Tier 0: fixed seat-to-pedal distance, reclined posture, pedals stay put
  • 5 Nm direct drive: smooth and detailed, still light
  • vs F1 Arcade: similar posture, far less rigid, no motion, weaker wheel

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: packs into a closet
  • +: real driving position
  • +: works in front of a couch TV
  • +: base, wheel, pedals all move to a rigid rig later
  • +: enough for years. r/simracing owners run 5 Nm on a folding stand and stay happy
  • −: flex under hard braking and above ~8 Nm (makers claim 10 to 13 Nm)
  • −: fabric seat sags over time
  • −: shifter mounts wobble
  • −: cables to manage every session
  • −: center post between the legs on some designs
  • −: the foldable itself has no upgrade path

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Load cell brake, set light. Foldables flex past ~25 to 30 kg
  • Then a rigid rig, once the space exists
  • Resale on the foldable ~half (est)

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• Playseat Challenge, NLR GTLite, F-GT Lite: common on Marketplace, ~$100 to $180 (est)
  • Check: seams and velcro, hinges lock under load, wheel plate holes match your base, no bent tubes
  • Avoid: no-name stands made for G29 only (thin plates crack with direct drive)

docs.title: $1,200–$1,600
docs.text: Assumes: existing PC/console, display, dedicated space

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• Permanent spot available
  • Drives weekly
  • Wants braking that is the same every lap
  • Skip if: you can stretch to Tier 3. Its rig and pedals are the buy-once choice
  • Skip if: it must pack away (Tier 1)

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• PC: Moza R9 V3 base $329 (9 Nm) + KS wheel $229 + SRP2 pedals $149 (entry load cell) + NLR GTRacer 2.0 cockpit $499 = ~$1,200
  • PC, better pedals: swap in Moza CRP2 $369 = ~$1,430
  • PC, on aluminum profile: swap the cockpit for a Trak Racer TR40S $349 + reclining seat $229 + brackets ~$60 = ~$1,350. The rig carries to Tier 3
  • PC, alt: Simagic Alpha Evo Sport 9 Nm bundle (base, wheel, pedals) ~$600 to $790 + cockpit
  • PlayStation: Fanatec GT DD Pro 8 Nm bundle $860 + load cell kit ~$100 to $140 + Fanatec CSL Cockpit with seat $400 = ~$1,400
  • PlayStation, alt: Logitech RS50 + RS pedals (load cell) ~$700 to $800 + GTRacer 2.0 $499 = ~$1,200 to $1,300
  • Xbox: Thrustmaster T598 Xbox $600 + GTRacer 2.0 $499 = ~$1,100, before a load cell
  • Xbox, alt: Fanatec CSL Cockpit bundle $1,045 (cockpit, seat, CSL DD 5 Nm, wheel, pedals). Confirm the wheel is Xbox licensed
  • Not included: screen and mount, shifter

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• ~130 to 140 × 60 to 70 cm of floor, permanent
  • Assembly 2 to 4 hours

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• vs Tier 1: nothing moves when you brake, so muscle memory forms
  • 8 to 9 Nm: real weight in fast corners
  • Load cell: brake by pressure, not pedal travel
  • Slower for the first sessions on a load cell, then more consistent
  • vs F1 Arcade: wheel detail equal or better, still no motion

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: biggest consistency jump per dollar
  • +: always ready to drive
  • +: base, wheel, pedals carry to Tier 3
  • −: tube frames have limited adjustment
  • −: some wheel deck flex above ~10 Nm
  • −: proprietary hole patterns and accessories
  • −: permanent floor space
  • −: a steel cockpit is replaced at Tier 3. A profile rig is not

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Better pedals: a mid load cell set
  • Then the rig itself, if on a steel cockpit
  • Seat can move across with brackets

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• Look for: Moza R9, Fanatec CSL DD 5 / 8 Nm, load cell pedals
  • New direct drive prices fell in 2026: used must be clearly under today's new price
  • Check: Fanatec QR1 vs QR2 (old QR1 does not fit current wheels), shaft play, brake reads smoothly to 100%
  • Avoid: belt bases priced near new direct drive, sellers who cannot show it working
  • Warranty usually does not transfer (Fanatec, Thrustmaster)

docs.title: $1,800–$2,200
docs.text:
Assumes: existing PC/console, display, dedicated space

  • With rig shipping and sales tax: up to ~$2,400

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• Committed, races weekly or in a league
  • Wants to stop upgrading
  • Skip if: under ~2 hours a week
  • Skip if: PlayStation and only Gran Turismo (Tier 2 gear on a better rig is enough)

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• PC: Moza R12 V2 base $429 (12 Nm) + KS wheel $229 + CRP2 load cell pedals $369 + Sim-Lab GT1 Evo rig $390 + seat and brackets ~$250 + monitor mount ~$100 = ~$1,770, plus rig shipping ~$100 to $250 (est)
  • PC, alt: Simagic Alpha Evo 12 Nm $549 + P1000 pedals $469 + GT Neo wheel ~$270 + same rig and seat = ~$1,930. Close to what newer F1 Arcade rigs use
  • PlayStation / Xbox / PC: Fanatec ClubSport DD+ GT3 bundle $1,405 (base, wheel, 3 load cell pedals) + GT1 Evo $390 + seat ~$250 = ~$2,045
  • Logitech route: PRO wheel 11 Nm $1,000 to $1,200 + PRO pedals $380 + rig + seat = ~$2,020 to $2,220
  • Other rigs: Trak Racer TR80S $499, RigMetal Plus $539, ASR 3 $550, NLR GTElite Lite $599
  • Rig prices exclude seat, brackets, slider, monitor mount
  • Not included: screen, shifter, handbrake

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• GT1 Evo frame: 135×58×66 cm
  • With seat, pedals, wheel: ~150×70 cm (est)
  • Plan ~2.0×1.0 m with a screen and room to get in
  • Assembly 3 to 6 hours, plus an evening of adjusting

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• vs Tier 2: zero flex, every angle adjustable
  • Brake you can stand on. Set it as firm as you like
  • 12 Nm: no clipping in normal use
  • vs F1 Arcade: wheel and pedals match or beat the venue's
  • Missing vs F1 Arcade: body motion, giant screens

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: rig and pedals are a 10-year purchase
  • +: everything bolts on later: shifter, shakers, motion
  • +: nothing is thrown away at Tier 4
  • −: industrial look
  • −: heavy, long assembly
  • −: many small extras: brackets, T-nuts, slider, bolts
  • −: popular rigs often back-ordered

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Display: triples or VR (Tier 4)
  • Not more torque

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• Aluminum profile rigs: best used buy in the hobby. Barely wear, costly to ship, so local pickup is cheap
  • Look for: Moza R12 / R16, Simagic Alpha, Fanatec ClubSport DD, Heusinkveld Sprint pedals
  • Check: 40-series profile (30-series is flimsy), all brackets and T-nuts, pedal controller box included
  • Avoid: wood or PVC rigs priced like aluminum, pedals missing elastomers

docs.title: $3,500–$5,500
docs.text:
Assumes: existing PC with a strong GPU. Displays included

  • GPU for triple 1440p: RTX 5070 Ti class, ~$860. Pimax Dream Air class VR: RTX 4090 / 5090

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• PC driver who wants peripheral vision and immersion
  • Rally and drift fans who need a shifter and handbrake
  • Skip if: mostly F1 25, Forza or EA WRC (they only stretch across triples)
  • Console: no triples. PlayStation has PS VR2 for Gran Turismo 7. Otherwise a big TV on a Tier 3 rig is the ceiling

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• Triples: Tier 3 PC build on a Sim-Lab P1X Pro rig $770 + clutch $99 + SHH HUBB shifter ~$150 + freestanding triple stand ~$275 + 3× 27" or 32" 1440p ~$600 to $900 + 2 bass shakers and amp ~$180 = ~$3,400 to $3,650
  • VR: same without stand and monitors + Meta Quest 3 $600 = ~$3,100
  • VR, sharper: Pimax Dream Air SE from $899, Dream Air from $1,999. Bigger GPU needed. See Displays
  • Top of band: 18 to 21 Nm base (Moza R21 Ultra $699), handbrake $99, OLED monitors ($300+ each)
  • PlayStation: Fanatec ClubSport DD+ bundle $1,405 + P1X Pro $770 + seat ~$250 + PS VR2 $399 = ~$2,800. Fanatec shifter ~$300 and handbrake ~$230 on top

docs.title: Triples vs VR
docs.text:
• Triples: 140 to 170° view, cars visible alongside, nothing on your face. Sit down and drive
  • VR: true depth and scale, no floor space. Hot, isolating, heavy on the GPU
  • r/simracing in 2026: more people move from VR to triples than back. Comfort, not picture
  • Try VR before buying. Quest 3S $350 is the cheap test
  • Triples need games that support them. F1 25, EA WRC and Forza only stretch
  • Monitors, headsets, full comparison: Displays

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• 27" triples: ~180 cm wide × 160 cm deep (est)
  • 32" triples: ~210 cm wide (est)
  • VR: same as Tier 3, ~150×70 cm
  • A full day including monitor alignment and software

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• Look into the apex, see the car next to you
  • Shakers: engine, kerbs, gear shifts through the seat
  • vs F1 Arcade: better view than the venue
  • vs F1 Arcade: the buzz, not the heave and pitch

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: biggest immersion jump per dollar
  • +: VR is the cheapest way to 1:1 scale
  • +: everything carries to Tier 5
  • −: GPU cost not in the total
  • −: triples eat a room
  • −: VR is hot and isolating
  • −: more software to maintain (SimHub, triple configs)
  • −: shakers travel through floors to neighbors

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Belt tensioner, then motion (Tier 5)
  • Optional: stronger base, active brake pedal. Feel, not lap time

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• Used monitors and triple stands: plentiful, low risk
  • Same model and revision matters more than price
  • Used Quest 3: ~$350 to $450 fair (est)
  • Check: dead pixels side by side, VR lens scratches, headset factory reset
  • Avoid: mixed monitor models, tight 1000R curves, sun-burned VR lenses

docs.title: $10,000–$18,000
docs.text:
Assumes: existing high-end PC, dedicated room. Displays included

  • "Motion lite" now exists at $7,000 to $9,000

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• This is the main hobby
  • Real-world drivers training
  • Chasing the F1 Arcade feel at home
  • Skip if: not yet consistent on Tier 3 or 4 (motion adds immersion, not pace)
  • Skip if: someone lives below you (actuators thump)

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• Full: Simucube 3 Pro base $1,599 (25 Nm) + wheel ~$1,000 (est) + Simucube ActivePedal Pro brake from $1,849 + throttle ~$400 (est) + D-BOX G5 4-actuator kit $6,200 to $8,250 + Sim-Lab P1X Ultimate rig $877 + seat ~$400 + 3× 32" ~$900 + stand ~$300 = ~$13,500 to $15,600
  • Motion lite: Moza R25 Ultra $899 + CS Pro wheel $329 + mBooster active pedal set $949 + Moza HMA150 4-actuator kit $2,999 + P1X Pro $770 + seat + 3× 27" + stand = ~$7,100
  • 2DOF, whole rig moves: Tier 4 build on an NLR Elite rig + Next Level Racing Motion Plus $2,799 = ~$6,500 to $7,500
  • PC only: motion reads PC telemetry
  • Add a belt tensioner: Qubic QS-BT1, $1,450 to $1,830. Owners with both rate it above motion alone. Buy it first
  • Not included: PC, pallet freight, software licenses

docs.title: F1 Arcade comparison
docs.text:
• F1 Arcade: Vesaro rigs, D-BOX G5 actuators, custom rFactor 2
  • Newer venues: Simagic Alpha Evo base, P1000 pedals, GT Neo wheel (per Simagic)
  • So the venue is Tier 5 motion with roughly Tier 3 controls
  • The D-BOX kit alone costs more than a whole Tier 4 rig
  • This tier: same motion family, stronger wheel, better pedals

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• ~210×180 cm with triples, plus clearance to move (est)
  • One to two days to build, weeks to tune

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• Chassis heaves, pitches, rolls (3DOF). No yaw: slides are hinted, not felt
  • Kerbs and gear shifts hit the whole body
  • Active brake: ABS pulse, pad feel, different per car
  • Not faster. More real

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: closest thing to the venue or a pro simulator
  • +: D-BOX and Simucube hold resale value
  • −: cost
  • −: noise and floor vibration
  • −: tuning time
  • −: little lap time gain
  • −: service means shipping heavy parts

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Nothing hardware
  • Coaching and seat time

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• Look for: Simucube 2 Sport / Pro (new $999 / $1,299), D-BOX Gen 3 to 5, Heusinkveld Ultimate+ pedals
  • Check: actuator knocking, controller box and cables present, motion software license transfers, E-stop works
  • Avoid: undocumented DIY motion, kits missing controller or brackets, sellers who won't demo under load

docs.title: Sound
docs.text:
• What: engine and tire noise

docs.title: What matters
docs.text:
• Nothing moves when you brake hard. Pedal end first, wheel deck second
  • Wheel deck and pedal deck that fit your gear's bolt pattern
  • Adjustability: seat, pedal and wheel distance and angle
  • Where the monitor goes
  • Whether it has to pack away. Pack-away rigs only get used if setup takes about a minute
  • Build quality: a tight, square 4080 rig beats a loose bigger one

docs.title: Ignore
docs.text:
• 40160 vs 4080 profile, below ~20 Nm. Not a performance upgrade for a beginner
  • Maker torque ratings on foldables. They say what it survives, not what stays stiff
  • Looks
  • Brand accessories. Profile rigs take anything with a T-nut

docs.title: Profile sizes
docs.text:
• The number is the beam cross-section in mm: 4080 = 40×80
  • 4080: fine to ~16 Nm. Enough for any first rig
  • 40120 / 40160: for 20 Nm+, very stiff pedals, motion
  • Price gap is small. Overbuying slightly is fine, not needed

docs.title: Real cost of a profile rig

  • Arrives in 2 to 3 heavy boxes. 3 to 6 hours to build
  • Popular rigs are often back-ordered. Check stock first

  • r/simracing in 2026: most switch stories go VR to triples, for comfort. Some switch back, many keep both

docs.title: What matters
docs.text:
• Distance: screen right behind the wheelbase. Closer beats bigger

  • Correct field of view. See First Setup
  • 120 to 165 Hz, held steady
  • Which games you play. Not all do triples properly
  • What your PC can drive. See PC / Console
    • Triple 1080p is about as heavy as one 4K screen

docs.text:
• 240 Hz and up

  • Tight 1000R curves for triples
  • HDR, at first

docs.text:
• Three identical monitors, thin bezels, VESA holes

  • A freestanding stand. Desk arms sag
  • Budget pick: AOC CQ32G4VE, 32" 1440p, 1500R, ~EUR 170 each
  • Also common: Samsung Odyssey G5 32" 1440p

docs.text:
Photo: dronepicr, CC BY 2.0, cropped

NEW PAGE

Added by Claude on 2026-10-09. Not in the original site plan. Keep, edit or delete.

  • What: add-ons that make you feel the car. shakers, belts, wind, motion
  • Why: immersion. not lap time
  • When: last. after rig, pedals, wheelbase, screens

docs.title: Buy order
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Bass shakers<br>$100+] --> B[Pedal haptics<br>$50+] --> C[Wind<br>$75+] --> D[Belt tensioner<br>$1,400+] --> E[Motion<br>$3,000+]

docs.title: Varieties
docs.text:
Add-on You feel Price Moves you? Bass shakers Engine, kerbs, shifts, wheel slip $100 to $350 No. Vibration only Pedal haptics ABS, lockup, wheelspin under your foot $50 to $150 a pedal No Wind Speed on your face. Also cooling in VR $75 to $400 No Belt tensioner Harness pulls tight under braking $1,400 to $1,800 Squeezes you G-seat Seat panels press into you in corners ~$3,000 Squeezes you Seat mover Seat tilts $1,500 to $3,000 Yes, 2DOF Actuators under the rig Whole rig tilts and lifts $3,000 to $9,000 Yes, 3DOF Traction loss, 6DOF Rear slides out, rig shifts sideways $4,500+ Yes, 4 to 6DOF
  • All of it is PC only. It runs on game telemetry
  • Exception: a shaker fed from the audio output works on console

docs.title: Bass shakers
docs.text:
• A speaker-like puck bolted to the seat or pedal plate. Plays the car as vibration
  • Not motion. Nothing moves, it buzzes and thumps
  • Driven by SimHub through a small amp
Level Kit Price Notes Starter Dayton puck (TT25) + small amp ~$50 to $80 Weak. Pedal plate or a light seat Default 1 or 2 Dayton BST-1 + small amp (Fosi, Nobsound) + SimHub ~$100 to $180 Best value. $180 covers two shakers, amp, USB sound card, wire, SimHub Stronger Dayton BST-300EX + bigger amp $199 a pair + amp Needs a rigid rig Plug and play ButtKicker Gamer Plus / Pro $280 / $350 Amp and clamp included Four corners 4 shakers + 4-channel amp $415 to $1,300 Left / right and front / rear effects. Diminishing returns
  • Best immersion per dollar in the hobby
  • Works on an office chair or foldable too
  • Mount on the seat, not the frame. Quieter, and you feel more
  • Rubber feet under the rig. Vibration travels through floors
  • First effects: RPM and gear shift. Then road bumps and kerbs
  • Each effect at 10 to 20%. Too many at once feels like noise
  • Four corners: you cannot tell the wheels apart. Still adds immersion
  • Not for everyone. Some send them back and keep pedal haptics

docs.title: Pedal haptics
docs.text:
• Small motor on the pedal. ABS and lockup on the brake, wheelspin on the throttle
  • Useful, not just fun: you feel the lock before you see it
  • Simagic P-HPR: $49 each plus power supply. Fits Simagic pedals, adapters exist for others
  • Cheap route: a Dayton puck under the pedal plate. Weaker than real pedal haptics
  • Active pedals (Simucube ActivePedal, Moza mBooster) do this and more. See Pedals

docs.title: Wind
docs.text:
• Fans on the rig. Speed follows the car's speed through SimHub
  • Best in VR: cools your face. Some find it eases nausea
  • DIY controller + PC fans: ~$75
  • Ready kits, two fans: $190 to $430 (SimRaceLab, RaceKraft)
  • A desk fan does half the job for free
  • Console: fans on a manual dial work without telemetry
  • Owners like it. Nobody calls it essential

docs.title: Belt tensioner
docs.text:
• Motors pull the harness tight under braking, loosen on throttle
  • Does what motion cannot: holds pressure for the whole braking zone
  • r/simracing: buy it before motion. Owners with both say the belt adds more on its own
  • Helps braking, not just immersion
  • Qubic QS-BT1: $1,450 to $1,830. Silent
  • DIY SimHub tensioner: under $1,000, noisy
  • SimXperience G-Belt: ~$1,365
  • Needs a bucket seat with harness slots and a 4 to 6 point harness

docs.title: Motion: the six directions
docs.text:
Axis Movement Feels like Pitch Nose tilts up / down Braking, acceleration Roll Tilts left / right Cornering load Heave Whole rig up / down Kerbs, bumps, crests Yaw Rear swings around The back stepping out Surge Slides forward / back Braking, acceleration, without tilting Sway Slides left / right Cornering, without tilting
  • DOF = degrees of freedom = how many of these a platform does

docs.title: 3DOF vs 6DOF
docs.text:
3DOF 6DOF Axes Pitch, roll, heave All six Hardware 4 actuators under the rig Hexapod, or 3DOF plus sliding base (surge, sway, traction loss) Price $3,000 to $9,000 $4,500 to $30,000+ (est) Space Rig footprint plus a little clearance Much more, in every direction Slides Hinted at through roll Felt directly through yaw Who Home rigs. The normal choice Enthusiasts with the room, pro simulators
  • In between
    • 2DOF: pitch + roll. Seat movers
    • 4DOF: 3DOF + rear traction loss (yaw). The useful middle step
  • Yaw is the upgrade that matters for drift, rally, catching slides
  • Surge and sway add little on their own
  • No home platform holds a sustained g-force. Motion gives the first hit, then eases back
  • More DOF is not automatically better. Most guides are written by sellers
  • Owners on r/simracing: "it's awesome but for fun, it's not going to make you faster"
  • DIY route: SFX100 actuators run from SimHub

docs.title: Motion levels
docs.text: Level Examples Price Notes 2DOF Seat movers: DOF Reality M2 $1,499, Next Level Racing Motion V3 $2,999. Whole rig: NLR Motion Plus $2,799 $1,500 to $3,000 Seat movers leave wheel and pedals still, which feels odd to some Affordable 3DOF Moza HMA150 $2,999, DOF Reality H3 $2,999 ~$3,000 The 2026 change. Motion at half the old price Premium 3DOF D-BOX G5 $6,000 to $8,250, Qubic QS-210 / QS-220 (EUR 6,680 / 8,880) $6,000 to $10,000 Faster, quieter, proven. D-BOX is what F1 Arcade uses 6DOF eRacing Lab RS Ultimate ~$4,500 + rig, DOF Reality H6 $6,999, pro hexapods $4,500 to $30,000+ (est) Room-sized commitment. Sliding parts add noise

docs.title: Moza HMA150
docs.text:
• Moza's first motion product: four actuators that bolt under an aluminum profile rig
  • $2,999, controller built in. About half the price of the D-BOX class
  • 3DOF: pitch, roll, heave. Carries 350 kg, rig and driver included
  • Shipping since Oct 2026. EU preorders mid-November
  • First owners: quiet for the driver, heard downstairs. Good build. Tiring to drive
  • Early review: one failed cable, loud first power supplies (since revised). Its built-in vibration does not replace shakers
  • Not there yet: SimHub support, VR motion compensation
  • Extra: "AI Motion" makes motion for games that send no telemetry
  • First generation. Long-term reliability unknown

docs.title: What matters
docs.text:
• Shakers: on the seat, few effects, kept low
  • Belt tensioner before motion
  • Motion: a rigid aluminum profile rig first. Motion on a flexy rig is wasted
  • Motion: speed and smoothness of the actuators, not travel
  • Motion: software. Game support, ease of tuning
  • Noise, and who lives below you
  • Cable clearance. Nothing may pinch as the rig moves
  • VR on a moving rig needs motion compensation set up, or the view drifts

docs.title: Ignore
docs.text:
• Lap time claims. A static rig is more repeatable under braking
  • Big travel numbers
  • 6DOF for a home rig
  • Motion before load cell pedals and a direct drive base
  • A harness without a tensioner. Decoration
  • Four-corner shakers, at first

docs.title: By tier
docs.text:
• Tier 0 to 2: none. A desk fan
  • Tier 3: one shaker under the seat
  • Tier 4: shakers on seat and pedals, wind if in VR
  • Tier 5: 3DOF motion, belt tensioner, shakers

docs.title: Used
docs.text:
• Shakers and amps: low risk. Nothing to wear out
  • Actuators: listen for knocking. Controller, cables, brackets all present
  • Ask if the motion software license transfers
  • Avoid: undocumented DIY motion

docs.text:
• What: runs the sim
  • Why: decides what you can play and how smooth
  • When: first. then stop thinking about it

docs.title: Choices
docs.text:
Platform Price new Good Bad PS5 $600 to $650, refurb $499. Pro $900 Gran Turismo 7, zero setup, PS VR2 Fewest wheels work, costs more at every tier Xbox Series S / X $500 / $750 to $800 Forza, Game Pass, Moza R3 works Forza Motorsport no longer updated PC, entry ~$1,150 Every sim, every wheel, all the free software Setup and tinkering PC, mid ~$1,850 to $2,200 Ultrawide, entry triples, Quest VR Price PC, high ~$3,200 Triple 1440p, most VR Price

  • Buying new only for sim racing: a PC is the better buy in 2026. Consoles went up
  • 2026: GPUs, RAM, consoles, VR headsets all cost more than older guides say

docs.title: PC levels
docs.text:
Level Parts class Runs Entry, ~$1,150 Ryzen 5 + RX 9060 XT 16 GB or RTX 5060 Single 1080p / 1440p Mid, ~$2,000 X3D CPU + RTX 5070 or RX 9070 XT Ultrawide, triple 1080p, Quest VR High, ~$3,200 9800X3D + RTX 5070 Ti to 5080 Triple 1440p, most VR
  • Sims with big grids lean on the CPU. An X3D chip matters more than usual
  • 12 to 16 GB of GPU memory for triples or VR. Not 8
  • Triple 1440p: RTX 5070 Ti is the sweet spot. The 5070 runs short of memory. 5080 for high refresh
  • Nvidia over AMD for triples: better triple-screen support in sims
  • Pimax Dream Air class VR: RTX 4090 / 5090. Above the "high" PC here
  • RTX 5090: far above list price in Oct 2026. Check before planning around one
  • Under ~$2,000, prebuilts are often cheaper than building right now
  • Older sims (Assetto Corsa, iRacing, RaceRoom) run on modest hardware

docs.title: What only PC can do
docs.text:
• iRacing, Le Mans Ultimate, Automobilista 2, BeamNG, AC EVO

docs.text: Type Reads Notes Potentiometer Pedal position, by a rubbing contact Wears, gets jumpy Hall Pedal position, by a magnet Same feel, lasts Load cell Force on the pedal The upgrade that matters Hydraulic Load cell or pressure sensor, with real fluid resistance On cheap sets "hydraulic" means a small damper Active A motor creates the resistance Not the same as vibration add-ons

docs.title: Why a load cell
docs.text:
• Real brakes respond to pressure
  • Your leg repeats a force far better than a foot position
  • Gain: the same braking every lap. Consistency first, speed after
  • Biggest for: braking at the limit without ABS, easing off while turning in
  • Slower for the first week or two. Normal

docs.title: What matters
docs.text:
• Load cell brake
  • A mount that does not move. Seat and pedals tied together
  • Adjustable stiffness (rubber stacks or springs)
  • Pedal spacing and angle that fit your feet
  • Console: must be the same brand as the wheelbase

docs.title: Ignore
docs.text:
• 200 kg vs 100 kg sensors. Nobody brakes above 60 to 80 kg
  • A clutch "just in case". Cheap to add later
  • Vibration motors sold as "active"
  • Active pedals, unless you change brake feel per car. A load cell plus pedal haptics gets most of the feel for a fraction of the money
  • Setting it as stiff as it goes
  • Inverted (hanging) pedals, unless you want road car feel and have the rig

docs.title: Two pedals or three
docs.text:
• Two is enough: F1, GT3, prototypes, most online racing
  • Clutch needed: H-pattern shifter, drifting, trucks, some standing starts
  • Add-on clutch: $45 to $100 on most sets

  • Best supply: barely used gear from people who went all in and quit
  • Seen paid: G29 $100 to $150, Moza R9 + load cell pedals EUR 350, PS VR2 EUR 150
  • Risky used buys: direct drive bases priced near new. New prices fell in 2026
  • Warranty rarely transfers (Fanatec and Thrustmaster say no). Price it as no warranty
  • Before paying
    • Powers on and calibrates
    • Every pedal and button registers
    • Power supply, cables, quick release, clamp all present
    • Video of it working in a game if not buying in person
  • Walk away from: shipping-only sellers with stock photos, gift card or friends-and-family payment, prices far under market

docs.text:
• Moza: everyday prices already match last Black Friday. Waiting saves little
  • Fanatec, Thrustmaster: 20 to 35% off in late November. Waiting pays
  • Logitech: discounted all year. Never pay list
  • 2026 is a bad year for anything with memory in it: GPUs, RAM, consoles, VR headsets are up
  • Monitors got cheaper

docs.title: Common regrets
docs.text:
• Buying endgame gear first. A 5 Nm base on a wheel stand lasts years
  • More torque before a load cell brake
  • A foldable, then a 12 Nm base six months later
  • A load cell set stiff on a rolling office chair. Block the chair, set it light
  • A wheel that does not work on your console
  • A formula wheel first, because of F1 Arcade. Miserable in road cars
  • Triples for F1 25 or Forza. They only stretch
  • Motion before a rigid rig
  • A Logitech G923 as an upgrade from a G29. Same thing
  • A mid-priced steel tube cockpit, replaced a year later
  • A clutch pedal that never gets used

docs.title: The two free wins
docs.text:
• Correct field of view (FOV)
  • Force feedback that does not clip

docs.title: Seating
docs.text:
• Wheel distance: shoulders on the seat, arm straight, wrist rests on top of the rim
  • Elbows bent ~90 to 120° at 9 and 3
  • Wheel height: top of rim around shoulder height
  • Pedals: knee still bent at full brake
  • Office chair: lock or cup the casters before anything else
  • GT position (upright, pedals low): start here. Works for everything
  • Formula position (reclined, feet high): only if you drive formula cars only

docs.title: Screen and FOV
docs.text:
• FOV = how much of the world is squeezed onto your screen
  • Game defaults are far too wide: everything looks slow and far, braking points are wrong
  • Correct FOV depends on two things: screen width and eye distance
  • Steps
    • Move the screen as close as possible, right behind the wheelbase
    • Screen center at or just below eye level
    • Measure eye-to-screen distance and screen width
    • Put the numbers in an FOV calculator, enter the result in the game
    • The calculator converts for each game. Some want degrees, some a slider value
  • Correct FOV feels zoomed in at first. Give it a few sessions
Screen Eyes at 60 cm 70 cm 100 cm 27" 53° 46° 33° 32" 61° 54° 39° 34" ultrawide 67° 59° 43° 49" super-ultrawide 90° 81° 62° 55" TV at 2.5 m 27°
  • Table: side-to-side view angle on a flat screen
  • A 27" monitor at arm's length shows twice what a 55" TV across the room does
  • VR: no FOV setup. Set eye spacing (IPD) instead

docs.title: Wheel rotation
docs.text:
• Set the wheel software to its maximum (900° or more)
  • Let the game match each car automatically (iRacing, ACC, Assetto Corsa, Le Mans Ultimate do)
  • Wrong if: the on-screen wheel does not match your hands

docs.title: Force feedback
docs.text:
• Force feedback is information about front tire grip, not a strength contest
  • Clipping: the game asks for more force than the wheel has. Everything strong feels the same, detail vanishes
  • Tuning order
    • Wheel software: 100% on Logitech and belt wheels. Direct drive: a comfortable peak, often 5 to 8 Nm
    • In game: lower gain until the heaviest corner stops maxing the meter
    • Turn off fake effects (kerb, engine, road rumble), add back to taste
  • Arms ache after 20 minutes: too strong
  • Change one setting at a time

docs.title: Brake and pedals
docs.text:
• Calibrate in the maker's software first, then in each game
  • Load cell: set 100% at a force you can repeat for a whole race, not your one-time max
  • Beginner range: 20 to 40 kg
  • Small deadzone at the bottom so a resting foot does not drag the brake
  • Pick socks or shoes and stick with one

docs.title: First weeks
docs.text:
• Slower than a controller for days to weeks. Normal
  • First car: Mazda MX-5 or any slow rear-wheel-drive car, short track
  • Consistency first, speed later
  • Sessions of 30 to 60 minutes
  • ABS and traction control are not cheating. Use what the real car has

docs.title: Comfort
docs.text:
• Motion sickness on a screen: usually wrong FOV or uneven frame rate
  • VR: start with 10 to 15 minutes, stop at the first nausea, use a fan
  • Heat: a fan aimed at you is the cheapest upgrade
  • Noise: rubber mat under the rig, headphones for sound

docs.title: Free software worth installing (PC)
docs.text:
• Crew Chief: voice spotter ("car left") and race engineer. Free
  • SimHub: dash on an old phone, drives bass shakers. Free, license from 8 EUR
  • Maker software: Moza Pit House, Fanatec app, Simagic SimPro, Logitech G HUB. Update firmware first

docs.title: Online basics
docs.text:
• Two ratings everywhere: one for speed, one for clean driving
  • Clean laps raise the safety rating. Crashes lower it
  • Ready for a first ranked race: 10 clean laps in a row, often 5 to 10 hours in
  • Survive lap 1
  • The overtaking car is responsible for a safe pass
  • Spun: hold the brake, wait for traffic, rejoin off the racing line
  • No retaliation. Report after the race
  • Leagues: same people every week, cleanest racing for beginners
